Ai Evals Ai Product Management Llm Evaluation Product Management are evals the new prd? Priyam 6 min read · Oct 18, 2026 -- Listen Share my thoughts on evals, vibes and shipping ai products that don’t embarrass you… Press enter or click to view image in full size this cover is so corny — it can fit for any blog at this point! I’ll be upfront. Up until a few months back, my understanding of “ testing ” an AI feature was simple. Ask it ten questions, take screenshots, and put them next to ChatGPT and Gemini on a slide. It felt rigorous. It was mostly vibes. Those screenshots only taught me to make answers prettier . Bolder headers, a cleaner summary. They never told us if a real user actually got what they came for. That’s when evals stopped being an ML team thing for me and became a product thing. wait, what do i mean by an “ai feature”? Any part of a product where the AI creates the answer, instead of following fixed rules. Ask it the same thing twice and you can get two different replies. You’ve probably used a bunch of these already: Zomato’s AI assistant suggesting what to eat Meta AI inside WhatsApp answering your questions YouTube’s “Ask” button answering questions about a video Whoop Coach turning your sleep and strain data into advice LinkedIn’s AI drafting your posts and messages And at work: Freshworks’ Freddy AI and Salesforce’s Agentforce answering support tickets Notion AI summarising your notes Microsoft Copilot drafting emails in Outlook These are where evals matter. The checkout button, OTP login or settings page in these same apps? No evals needed. They do the exact same thing every time, and conventional testing handles them fine. okay, so what is an eval? I think of it as an exam for the product. You write the questions. You decide what a good answer looks like. Then you grade every answer the same way, every time something changes. If you’ve done regular product work, you already know its cousins: test cases, acceptance criteria, the QA checklist before a release. An eval is the same idea, made for software that doesn’t behave the same way repeatedly (thanks for generative AI). A normal button either works or it doesn’t. An AI feature can give a great answer on Monday and a wrong one on Tuesday, to the same question. Mind you, the “wrong” and “great” here can have weak, yet make-or-break differences. So you can’t test it once and move on. The idea isn’t new. Machine learning teams have always kept aside some examples the model never saw, and tested it on those. That’s roughly where benchmarks come from. What’s new is who needs this. Now that every product team ships AI features, every product team needs its own exam, built around its own users. The way I see it, a PRD says what good looks like. An eval checks every day whether you got there. why this is a pm’s job Here’s what surprised me. Writing an eval is mostly a product decision, not a technical one. To write one, one has to answer questions like: what does a good answer feel like to this user? Who is the user? Is short response better than complete? Should the AI ask a follow-up, or just answer? and so on… An engineer can build the testing setup. A data scientist can tune the scoring. But deciding what “good” means for a first-time AI user in a small town, versus a power user in a metro, is a product call. If the PM doesn’t make it, someone else will, by accident. There’s a second, more selfish reason. Evals help you say no . A lot of AI roadmaps I’ve seen start with “let’s build something custom for this.” A good eval tells you if the basic model already does the job well enough. If it does, you’ve just saved your team a lot of work. In my opinion, that’s one of the most useful things a PM can bring to an AI team. how to write one though? Don’t start with tools. Start by reading what your AI says, a lot of it, and noting down what goes wrong. On day one, that list is your first eval. Then start from the user and their objectives. Write their goal in their words, like “catch me up on today’s news” or “summarise this contract for me”. Add a couple of lines on what a good experience feels like. Next, break “good” into a few simple checks. Let’s call them graders : one or two words for what the user gets, like accurate , relevant or easy to read . Some matter more than others, so decide which ones count most. Keep each check simple. A plain pass/fail is often clearer than a score out of five, but I believe that call best depends on the respective product. And write it from the user’s side. “The user isn’t overwhelmed” works better than “uses exactly three bullets”. Then set the scope . What exactly are you testing: one question, a full chat, or a whole task from start to end? Pick what real users actually do. For a chat product, the first few messages usually tell you a lot more than a single question. Decide what to compare against. Your last version, the basic model, a competitor, or all three. A score means very little on its own. To score at scale, use an AI as the judge, but keep people in the loop. Even strong AI judges agree with humans only about 80% of the time , and they tend to prefer longer answers. So people check a sample by hand to keep the LLM judge honest in general. Finally, make it a gate, rather than a report. Every change runs the same set of tests across product. That way, fixing one thing while breaking three others gets caught before users find it. And every new failure you spot in real life gets added to that set.
